# Vector Spaces {#sec-vector_spaces}

## Real Vector Spaces {#sec-real_vector_spaces}

::: {#def-vectorspace}
**[Real vector space]{style="color: red;"}**

A real vector space is a set $\b{V}$ on which the two operations of $\cdot + \cdot : \b{V}\times \b{V} \to \b{V}$ (addition) and $\cdot * \cdot: \b{V}\times \b{R}\to \b{V}$ (scalar multiplication) are defined and satisfies the following properties: {#def-vector_space}
:::

1.  $\b{u}+\b{v}=\b{v}+\b{u}$ for all $\b{u},\b{v} \in \b{V}$
2.  $\b{u}+(\b{v}+\b{z})= (\b{u}+\b{v})+\b{z}$ for all $\b{u}, \b{v}, \b{z} \in \b{V}$
3.  $(ab)\b{v} = a(b\b{v})$ for all $v \in \b{V}$ and all $a,b \in \b{R}$
4.  There exists a zero element $\bs{0}_{\b{V}}$ or simply $\bs{0}$ when there is no risk of confusion, such that $\bs{0} + \b{v} = \b{v}$ for all $\b{0}, \b{v} \in \b{V}$
5.  For every $\b{v} \in \b{V}$, there exists $\b{v}' \in \b{V}$ such that $\b{v} + \b{v}' = \bs{0}$
6.  $1\b{v} = \b{v}$ for all $\b{v} \in \b{V}$
7.  $a(\b{u}+\b{v}) = a\b{u} + a\b{v}$ for all $a,b \in \b{R}$ and all $\b{u},\b{v} \in \b{V}$
8.  $(a+b)\b{v} = a\b{v} + b\b{v}$ for all $a,b \in \b{R}$ and all $\b{u},\b{v} \in \b{V}$

We can show identities such as $-1 * \b{v}=\b{v}'$ and $0 * \b{v}=\b{0}$ from the above axioms.

$$
\begin{align}
\pr{1+(-1)}\b{v}&=1*\b{v}+(-1)*\b{v}\\
\pr{0}\b{v}&=1*\b{v}+(-1)*\b{v}\\
\b{0}&=1*\b{v}+(-1)*\b{v}\\
\b{0}&=\b{v}+(-1)*\b{v}\\
(-1) * \b{v}&=\b{v}'
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
\pr{1+0} * \b{v}&=1 * \b{v}+(0) * \b{v}\\
\pr{1} * \b{v}&=1 * \b{v}+(0) * \b{v}\\
\b{v}&=\b{v}+(0) * \b{v}\\
\b{0}&=(0)*\b{v}\\
\end{align}
$$

When there is no confusion we will skip explicity writing $*$, so expressions such as $a * \pr{b \b{v}}=\pr{ab}  *  \b{v}$ will appears as $a\pr{b \b{v}}=\pr{ab}  \b{v}$

Examples of real vector spaces include the set of real numbers $\b{R}$ itself and the set of polynomials of order $k$.

::: {#def-subspace}
**[Subspace]{style="color: red;"}**

A subset $\b{U}$ of $\b{V}$ is a *subspace* of $\b{V}$ if it is also a vector space using the same addition and scalar operation as on $\b{V}$. 
Namely, $\b{U}$ only if it satisfies, $\b{0} \in \b{U}$, $\b{u} + \b{v} \in \b{U}$ for all $\b{u}, \in \b{U}$ and $a \b{u} \in \b{U}$ for all $a \in \b{R}$ and $\b{u} \in \b{U}$.
:::

## Finite Dimensional Vector Spaces {#sec-Finite_dimensional_vector_space}

A *list* of length $n$ is an ordered collection of $n$ elements. We denote lists without parenthesis as $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}$. By definition, a list has finite length.

A *linear combination* of a list of vectors $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \b{V}$  is a vector of the form $a_{1} \bs{v}_{1} + ... + a_{n} \bs{v}_{n}$ where $a_{1},...,a_{n} \in \b{R}$. 

The *span* of a list of vectors $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \b{V}$ is the set of all linear combinations of the form $a_{1} \bs{v}_{1} + ... + a_{n} \bs{v}_{n}$ where $a_{1},...,a_{n} \in \b{R}$ and is denoted by $\text{span}\pr{\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}}$. If $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}$ spans $\b{V}$, then $\text{span}\pr{\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n}} = \b{V}$


::: {#def-Finite_dimensional_vector_space}
**[Finite dimensional vector space]{style="color: red;"}**

A vector space $\b{V}$ is *finite dimensional* if some list of vectors $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \b{V}$ spans the space. 
:::

A list of vectors $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \b{V}$ is said to be *linearly independent* if its linear combination is $\bs{0}$ iff the scalars $a_{1},...,a_{n}$ are all $0$. On the contrary, a list is linearly dependent if a linear combination is $\bs{0}$ for some list of scalars $a_{1},...,a_{n}$ where not all are $0$. In a finite-dimensional vector space, the length of each linearly independent list of vectors is less than or equal to the length of every spanning list of vectors.

::: {#def-basis}
**[Basis]{style="color: red;"}**

A *basis* of $\b{V}$ is a linearly independent list of vectors $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \b{V}$ that spans $\b{V}$. An equivalent definition is that the list $\bs{v}_{1},...,\bs{v}_{n} \in \b{V}$ is *basis* of $\b{V}$ iff every $\bs{v} \in \b{V}$ can be written as a unique linear combination of the list.
:::

Every finite dimensional vector space $\b{V}$ has a basis. The *dimension* of $\b{V}$ is given by the length of any of its basis. All bases of a finite dimensional vector space have the same length. A proper subspace always has a smaller dimension than the larger space. We will denote finite dimensional vector spaces with a superscript to indicate the dimension, for example, $\b{V}^{n}$ or $P^{k}$.

## Real Inner Products and Norms {#sec-inner_prod_normed_spaces}

::: {#def-inner_prod}
**[Inner product]{style="color: red;"}** 

An *inner product* on $\b{V}$ is an operation $\apr{\cdot, \cdot} : \b{V} \times \b{V} \rightarrow \b{R}$ such that for all $\bs{u}, \bs{v}, \bs{z} \in \b{V}$ and for $a \in \b{R}$, we have

1. $\apr{\bs{u}, \bs v} = \apr{\bs v, \bs u}$
2. $\apr{\bs u, \bs v + a \bs z} = \apr{\bs u, \bs v} + a \apr{\bs u, \bs z}$
3. $\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u} \geq 0$
4. $\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u} = 0$ iff $\bs{u} = \bs{0}$
:::    

An real inner product space is a real vector space on which an inner product is defined.

::: {#def-norm}
**[Norm]{style="color: red;"}** 

A *norm* on $\b{V}$ is an operation $\norm{\cdot} : \b{V} \rightarrow \b{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that such that for all $\bs{u}, \bs{v} \in \b{V}$ and for $a \in \b{R}$, we have

1. $\norm{a \bs u} = \abs{a} \norm{\bs u}$
2. $\norm{\bs u + \bs v} \leq \norm{\bs u} + \norm{\bs v}$
3. $\norm{\bs u} = 0$ iff $\bs u = \bs 0$
:::

A vector space equipped with a norm is called a normed vector space. To be more precise, we denote a norm of vector space $\b{V}$ as $\norm{\cdot}_{\b{V}}$ and similarly for norms of other vector spaces. Every inner product induces a norm. The induced norm is given by $\norm{\bs u} = \sqrt{\inpd{\bs u}{\bs u}}$.

## Real Euclidean Space {#sec-euclidean_space}

::: {#def-euclidean_vector_space}
An **[Euclidean vector space]{style="color: red;"}** is a finite dimensional real inner product space, whose inner product is the dot product.
:::

The Euclidean norm is induced by the dot product.
